note: Straight-chain, acyclic hydrocarbons only. Formulas, names and structures are generated by lab-core.js and checked by scripts/validate-organic.cjs.

families.name: Alkanes
families.definition: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons. Every carbon-carbon bond is a single bond, so each carbon holds as many hydrogen atoms as it can.
features: Saturated: no C=C or C≡C bond
properties: Relatively unreactive compared with alkenes and alkynes.
Burn in air or oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water.
Do not dissolve in water; they mix with other non-polar liquids.
Boiling point rises as the chain gets longer.
families.reactionNote: In ultraviolet light a hydrogen atom of methane is replaced by chlorine.

families.name: Alkenes
families.definition: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons. They contain at least one carbon-carbon double bond, so they hold fewer hydrogen atoms than the alkane with the same number of carbons.
features: At least one carbon-carbon double bond (C=C)
Unsaturated: can take part in addition reactions
General formula CnH2n (acyclic, one double bond)
properties: More reactive than alkanes because of the double bond.
Undergo addition reactions with hydrogen, halogens, hydrogen halides and steam.
Small alkenes can join together to form polymers.
Burn in air, usually with a smokier flame than alkanes.
families.reactionNote: Hydrogen adds across the double bond, using a nickel catalyst.

families.name: Alkynes
families.definition: Alkynes are unsaturated hydrocarbons. They contain at least one carbon-carbon triple bond, so they hold even fewer hydrogen atoms than alkenes.
features: At least one carbon-carbon triple bond (C≡C)
Unsaturated: can take part in addition reactions
General formula CnH2n−2 (acyclic, one triple bond)
properties: More reactive than alkanes because of the triple bond.
Undergo addition reactions; with enough hydrogen they form alkanes.
Ethyne burns with a sooty flame in air; in pure oxygen the flame is very hot and is used in welding.
families.reactionNote: With a nickel catalyst, ethyne takes up two molecules of hydrogen to give ethane (via ethene).
